explanation:
## The predicate

```cpp
bool isPrime(int n)
{
    if (n < 2) return false;
    for (int i = 2; i * i <= n; ++i)
        if (n % i == 0) return false;
    return true;
}
```

Three lines, and each one is a decision worth naming.

**`if (n < 2) return false;`** handles 1, 0 and every negative in one test. It
has to come first: without it, `1` falls into the loop, `2 * 2 <= 1` is false
immediately, the loop body never runs, and the function returns `true` - so `1`
is reported prime. That single missing line is the commonest bug in this
function, and it is why `1 1` is a visible case rather than a hidden one.

**`return false` the moment a divisor is found.** The alternative is a flag:

```cpp
bool prime = true;
for (int i = 2; i * i <= n; ++i)
    if (n % i == 0) prime = false;     // keeps looking, pointlessly
return prime;
```

That works and does more work than it needs to. An early return out of a
predicate is clearer *and* faster, because the answer cannot change once a
divisor exists. The habit generalises: a function that has found its answer
should say so.

**`return true` at the end** is reachable only when no divisor was found, which
is the definition.

## Why `i * i <= n`

Divisors come in pairs. If `d` divides `n` then so does `n / d`, and one of
those two is always at or below the square root. So any composite number has a
divisor at or below its square root, and once `i` passes that point there is
nothing left to find.

```
n = 36:   1x36   2x18   3x12   4x9   6x6   |   9x4   12x3   18x2   36x1
                                      ^ sqrt(36)
                                      everything right of here is a mirror
```

For `n` = 100000 that is 316 divisions instead of 99998 - a factor of 300, from
one changed loop condition.

`i * i <= n` rather than `i <= std::sqrt(n)` avoids floating point entirely. The
square root of a perfect square can land a hair below the integer in `double`,
and then the last divisor is never tested: `sqrt(49)` coming back as 6.9999999
would make 49 look prime. Integer multiplication has no such failure mode. The
cost is that `i * i` must not overflow, which is why the statement caps `b`.

## The main loop

```cpp
for (int n = a; n <= b; ++n)
{
    if (isPrime(n))
    {
        ++count;
        largest = n;
        found = true;
    }
}
```

`largest` is simply overwritten each time, because the loop counts upward and
the last prime seen is the largest. No comparison is needed - the loop order
provides it. Worth noticing when it applies, and worth not assuming when it
does not.

## Why `found` instead of checking `largest`

```cpp
if (largest != 0) std::cout << "largest " << largest << "\n";   // fragile
```

It reads `largest == 0` as "there were none", which only works because 0 is not
prime. The reasoning is correct here and breaks the moment the values change -
the classic in-band sentinel problem, where a legitimate value and "no value"
share a representation.

`bool found` keeps the two separate, and `count != 0` would do just as well
since it is already being maintained. In modern C++ the type for this is
`std::optional<int>`, which makes "a value or nothing" unmistakable in the
signature rather than in a comment.

## The cases, and what each one breaks

| Input | Answer | What it catches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `1 1` | none | the missing `n < 2` guard |
| `2 2` | 2 | treating all even numbers as composite |
| `-10 1` | none | negatives, and a range entirely below 2 |
| `-5 3` | 2, 3 | a range *crossing* 2 |
| `8 9` | none | two composites, one even, one odd square |
| `1 100` | 25 primes | the standard sanity check |
| `2 100000` | 9592 | that the loop bound really is the square root |

The last one is a performance test disguised as a correctness test. With
`i < n` instead of `i * i <= n` the answer is still right, and on this range it
does roughly five billion divisions - enough to hit the three-second limit and
report a timeout instead of a wrong answer.
